problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-2x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-4y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.

feedback.problem: The function ${y}_{1}(t)={t}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation ${t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2y=0$ for $t>0.$ If ${y}_{2}=u(t){y}_{1}(t)$ is a second solution of the equation, then which of the following equations must be satisfied by $u(t)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We're given that

$$
{y}_{2}(t)=u(t){y}_{1}(t)=u{t}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u{t}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{t}^{2}+2ut \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u)-2u{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t+2u-2u) & =0 \\ {t}^{2}({u}^{″}{t}^{2}+4{u}^{′}t) & =0 \\ {t}^{3}({u}^{″}t+4{u}^{′}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${t}^{3}\ne 0$ for $t>0,$ we must have

$$
t{u}^{″}+4{u}^{′}=0.
$$
